There is a big difference between those who oppose vaccinations and those who oppose genetically modified organisms in my mind.

Vaccines have a huge amount of studies and clinical research to show that they are safe over the years. We can definitively prove that over 20 years vaccines are safe and effective with no long-term side effects. Those who oppose them choose to willfully ignore scientific evidence.

Genetically modified organisms do not have that same body of research behind them, and there are still huge gaps in our knowledge of genetics and how DNA is actually expressed in the cell. What they are doing is changing the genotype of an organism; we do not know all the details of how that changes the phenotype of the cell. For example, what if a random mutation to a gene three chromosomes over changes the protein expression of our modified gene and suddenly what was a healthy cell is now producing a mild toxin? It may only have a 0.0001% chance of happening, but it's still something we should identify from a scientific standpoint. The problem is we have a general lack of scientific evidence from independent sources.

Essentially, anyone really educated in the area should see that genetically modified organisms are *probably* safe, but we just don't have the volumes of scientific data to back that up. Also, if you look into the funding climate for this research, there is a huge squeeze in public funding for genetically modified organisms, and because of the opposition lobby, the cost associated with research is going up. So now the only people who can afford to do the research are the ones creating the organisms in the first place. That is why I'm nervous about genetically modified organisms.

We need ongoing continual research into the long-term effects of genetically modified organisms on public health. The funding should come from public entities so that we have unbiased research into long-term health. Currently, the only people who are doing the studies to say it's safe are the corporations who are creating these, and they do not have an incentive to continue research on the long-term effects. Odds are it's safe, but we need continual research to ensure it's safe over the long road. The last thing we want is to find out 50 years later that a substance actually does cause cancer.

The opposition lobby took these legitimate scientific concerns and just ran with it...but the reality is there is some truth to their underlying concerns even if they can't express it.

tl;dr: It's not the genetically modified organisms themselves, it's the funding climate around the scientific research into them.

I'll say my spouse actually has a PhD in Neuroscience and works in addiction research, so while I may not be an expert myself, it's impossible for me not to be very familiar with the subject.

I will start by saying that I agree most pro-legalization arguments tend to gloss over the side effects on their path to legalization. There are dangers and risks, especially for heavy chronic use, but I believe that you are overstating them and that it's no riskier than things that are currently legal.

1a.) Marijuana is addictive, contrary to popular belief.

Yes, you are absolutely correct. THC can be addictive, especially if used in adolescence. Biochemically, addiction is addiction, and there isn't much difference between addiction to heroin, alcohol, gambling, and addiction to THC. However, it's important to point out that THC doesn't directly activate the addiction pathways like, say, cocaine or tobacco. Therefore, when someone says weed isn't addictive, they can be both correct and wrong at the same time. The more appropriate thing to say would be that weed isn't any more addictive than other legally available substances. Unfortunately, that's a little too much nuance for a political statement, so instead "weed isn't addictive" is what people go with.

1b.) Lives have been destroyed by the previously stated addiction, without the involvement of legal issues.

Agree, addiction destroys lives. However, you are using humans as an example who are more complex than simply blaming one item for their problems. The individuals you mentioned may have underlying issues like depression that they are self-medicating with weed. There isn't much difference between addiction to alcohol to curb depression and addiction to THC. I absolutely agree we should have a focus on mental health for all addictions. At least you are consistent that if we keep marijuana illegal, we should also make alcohol and tobacco illegal, but I disagree that a general mental health argument should be linked to a legal policy of prohibition.

2.) Extremely slow cognitive function.

Unfortunately, we don't have a lot of studies on the long-term effects of THC because the classification of THC makes it very difficult to actually study. The intelligence argument is kind of tough to make. A better argument to make your case would be that long-term chronic use of THC has a negative effect on short-term memory. So yes, anyone who says there aren't long-term side effects to chronic abuse of marijuana isn't telling the truth. However, if we are going to make that statement, then it's also important to ensure we are dealing with chronic use, which doesn't necessarily relate to general recreational use.

However, once again from a legal policy standpoint, it's hard to argue that these side effects are any worse than other legally allowed substances. Long-term alcohol use leads to psoriasis, and long-term tobacco use leads to cancer. Yet both of those other substances are legally allowed to be abused. Once again, a more appropriate pro-legalization point would be that the long-term effects of marijuana are no worse than other legally allowed substances.

I think our discussion of whether we should or should not legalize marijuana (recreational usage) is being talked about incorrectly.

I don't think the current discussions are necessarily incorrect, but the nuances of the debate are generally lost in our sound bite media and typical pro-legalization advocates. The points you raise are good ones, but I don't believe they support continued prohibition. I'll see if I can answer your questions:

Is it ethical to allow easier access to marijuana for anyone (over the limitation, which I believe is usually 21+)?

I would say it's just as ethical to allow marijuana as it is to allow alcohol. It's pretty much universally agreed that you should be 21+ to legally purchase weed for good reasons. The counterargument is that if it became more readily available, kids would have easier access to weed and therefore be more likely to abuse it. This assumes, however, that weed isn't already available to kids just in school, which is a naive standpoint, and examination of the data in one state showed that there hasn't been an increase in underage smoking.

If we DO legalize marijuana for recreational use, can we put up safeguards to minimize addiction and destructive behavior from happening?

Yes, the same way we have safeguards in place for tobacco and alcohol.

If we DO NOT legalize marijuana for recreational use, when can we start discussing alcoholism, how rampant it is in a major city, and discover a potential fix to not only minimize the amount of alcoholism that exists but also provide help to people trying to escape what they consider to be a harsh reality?

I would LOVE to see us talking about more mental health assistance, including addiction treatment. However, I have a hard time linking a general mental health debate to the prohibition of a substance. We can't treat mental health through prohibition.

I see where you are coming from with your points, but I think you are inappropriately linking prohibition to mental health.
